tolerance_html:
mechloop/tolerance/process.py holds, per process, the standard deviations the tolerance verifier built its 3000 simulated machines with. The sheets hold the fabricator to +/-2 standard deviations of the same figures, so a batch of parts inside the drawing tolerance is the population that was simulated. A part AT the limit everywhere is worse than what was simulated: the limits are not a licence to sit on them.

printing_html:
• Printer assumed by the manufacture verifier: build volume (220.0, 220.0, 220.0), nozzle 0.4 mm, layer 0.2 (the verifier default: the design does not declare one) mm.
  • Orientation: pinned per part in the design (print_up), listed below; the STL is already turned so the bed face is on Z = 0.
  • Walls and infill: not declared by the design. The verifier's mass and time estimate used: estimate: 1.2 mm walls, 20% infill, 5 mm3/s, no support material counted.
  • The FEA load cases treat every printed part as solid, isotropic material. A part printed at 20 % infill is not the part that was analysed. For the parts with a load case (nut_block, nut_block_fr, x_belt_block, z_drive_mount, z_pedestal_fr), print solid or accept that the factor of safety is unverified.
  • No threads in plastic, no heat-set inserts: every screw in a printed part runs into a steel nut (captive pockets and slots are in the models).
  • Printed holes are drawn oversize (M3 4.2, M5 6.0) for an assumed 0.15 mm shrink; bearing seats are drawn 22.4 for a 22 mm bearing on the same assumption.

open_items.rank_label: would stop the build (or is a safety matter)
open_items.title: Lead screws: plain T8 thread in 608 bearings, pulley set screws carry the bed, nothing holds a screw down
open_items.known: Each catalogue screw is a plain threaded T8 bar, 300 mm, no machined journals. It stands in two 608 bearings on its thread crests (the fit is 'catalogue fit, trusted', not simulated), the 8 mm-bore pulley is set-screwed onto the thread and its hub on the upper bearing's inner ring carries that screw's share of the bed (10 to 20 N). Nothing but weight holds the screw DOWN: an upward push on the bed or a nut that binds while the bed descends lifts the screw out of its seats. The pulley's hub must clear the 608's outer ring (about 18 mm at most, per docs).
open_items.check: buy one screw, one pulley and two bearings first: check the screw's real outside diameter in the 608 bore, that the hub bears on the inner ring only, and that two set screws on a threaded surface hold 3 x the load; consider screws with turned ends and a collar under the lower bearing

The design note gives about 190 MPa in a class 12.9 screw as a hand estimate; no verifier computed it, and fatigue is not checked by anything. With fully threaded posts (see the thread-length item) the bending is on the thread root, which is worse than a plain shank.
open_items.check: after 20 heat cycles on the real machine: jam nuts still tight, tram unchanged within 0.05 mm, no visible bend

open_items.title: Bed on four slender posts: its own vibration was never analysed
open_items.known: No modal case exists for the plate on its posts and tie. The twin's resonance figures are for the toolhead and gantry only.
open_items.check: tap test / accelerometer on the bed plate during commissioning; ringing visible in Y at the print's base would point here

open_items.title: Lead differences between the three screws
open_items.known: A belt holds the screws to one angle, not one height. Rolled T8 screws differ in lead; no figure is in the catalogue (the harness assumes 0.02 mm between screws).
open_items.check: commissioning step M7 measures it; buy the three screws from one batch

open_items.title: Printed PETG mounts under steady load
open_items.known: Pedestals and drive mount carry the bed and the belt pull for years; creep is not modelled; bearing seats are printed.
open_items.check: re-check belt tension and tram after the first 50 hours

open_items.title: 2 mm steel Y motor and idler mounts
open_items.known: Their stiffness under 37 N of belt pull is in no FEA case, and the Y motor's allowed shaft load is read from one terse drawing line ('LENGTH 20mm: 21N MAX') whose meaning is inferred.
open_items.check: ask the motor's maker what that line means; watch for the Y pulleys tilting when the belts are tensioned

open_items.title: Part cooling is not modelled

open_items.title: Probe mount: stiffness and heat

open_items.check: bench step B1 with the sensor IN its mount with both nuts fitted, not bare

open_items.title: Report warning, manufacture `load_across_layers`
open_items.known: z_drive_mount: load case 'z_drive_mount_thrust' acts 100% along the build direction (-Z up): it pulls the layers apart, the weakest direction of a printed part, and the FEA assumes the material is equally strong every way.
open_items.check: Print with -Y up so the load runs along the layers, or add a through bolt that puts the layers in compression. (Direction only: a bending load across a tall part also loads the layers and is not detected.)

open_items.title: No lead-in chamfer on any hand-assembled bore (10 features)
open_items.known: The model has no chamfers at all (no cone faces on any custom part): bearing seats, the sleeve's bore, the probe's hole and the idler axles' holes start with a sharp edge. List below.
open_items.check: add 0.5 x 45 degree lead-ins on the drawings or break the edges by hand

open_items.title: Sharp edges: the model has almost no fillets and no chamfers
open_items.known: Every laser-cut and machined part is drawn with sharp edges and corners. The drawings carry the note 'Deburr; break all sharp edges 0.2-0.5 mm; outside profile corners R1 min unless dimensioned', which is NOT yet in the CAD. The Y belts pass through laser-cut slots in 3 mm steel: a burr there cuts the belt.
open_items.check: deburr everything; stone the belt slots
